questions.question: What must be true for a finite list $\mathcal V$ to be a spanning list for $V$?
options: $\mathcal V$ contains exactly one vector.
$V=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal V)$.
$\operatorname{span}(\mathcal V)=\{\boldsymbol 0\}$ only.
Every vector in $\mathcal V$ has length $1$.

questions.question: Does a spanning list have to be free of redundancy?
options: Yes, otherwise it cannot span.
No, it may contain redundant vectors.
No, because it cannot contain more than one vector.
Yes, every spanning list is automatically a basis.

questions.question: What does a spanning list guarantee about every vector in $V$?
options: Every vector in $V$ has a unique length.
Every vector in $V$ is a linear combination of the list.
Every vector in $V$ is orthogonal to the list.
Every vector in $V$ is one of the listed vectors.

questions.question: Which extra property turns a spanning list into a basis?
options: Containing infinitely many vectors.
Linear independence.
Having a zero vector in the list.
Being written in increasing order.

questions.question: Why is the word “finite” part of the definition of a spanning list here?
options: The field must contain finitely many scalars.
The vector space itself must contain finitely many vectors.
The definition uses a finite collection of vectors.
Only finite-dimensional spaces can contain zero.

questions.question: Does $((1,0),(0,1))$ span $\mathbb R^2$?
options: Yes, but only for vectors with positive coordinates.
No, because it has only two vectors.
No, because neither vector is $(1,1)$.
Yes, every $(a,b)$ equals $a(1,0)+b(0,1)$.

questions.question: Does $((1,0),(0,1),(1,1))$ span $\mathbb R^2$?
options: No, because three vectors cannot span a two-dimensional space.
No, because a spanning list cannot contain redundant vectors.
Yes, but only if $(1,1)$ is removed.
Yes, because the first two vectors already span $\mathbb R^2$.

questions.question: Does $((1,0))$ span $\mathbb R^2$?
options: Yes, because $(1,0)$ is nonzero.
Yes, one nonzero vector spans every vector space.
No, because it does not contain the zero vector.
No, it only spans the $x$-axis.

questions.question: Which list spans the $x$-axis in $\mathbb R^2$?
options: $((1,0),(0,1))$ only if the target is the $y$-axis

questions.question: Does the list $((0,0))$ span $\mathbb R^2$?
options: Yes, because every spanning list must contain zero.
No, because zero vectors cannot be in any span.
No, its span is only $\{(0,0)\}$.
Yes, because it contains the zero vector.

questions.question: What is the difference between a spanning list and a basis?
options: A spanning list is always smaller than a basis, in all instances without exception.
A basis does not have to span the space.
A basis spans and is linearly independent; a spanning list may be redundant.
A spanning list cannot contain nonzero vectors.

questions.question: If a vector is removed from a spanning list, what can happen?
options: The remaining list may or may not span, depending on the removed vector's redundancy.
The vector space stops being finite-dimensional, universally and without exception.
The remaining list can never span.
The remaining list must always span.

questions.question: What does a finite-dimensional vector space have according to the spanning-list result?
options: Only one vector.
A finite spanning list.
Only the zero vector.
No basis.

questions.question: Which list spans $\mathbb R^2$?
Which list does not span $\mathbb R^2$?
Using the spanning list $((1,0),(0,1),(1,1))$, how can $(3,4)$ be generated?
Can a list with more vectors than necessary still be a spanning list?
options: Yes, spanning allows redundancy.
No, extra vectors always destroy spanning.
Only if all extra vectors are zero.
Only if the vector space is one-dimensional.

questions.question: If a basis of $V$ is enlarged by adding one extra vector from $V$, what is usually true of the enlarged list?
options: It no longer contains vectors from $V$.
It becomes a smaller basis.
It still spans $V$ but is redundant.
It stops spanning $V$.

questions.question: Does $((1,0,0),(0,1,0))$ span $\mathbb R^3$?
options: Yes, because $\mathbb R^3$ has three coordinates.
No, vectors with nonzero third coordinate cannot be generated.
No, because the list contains no zero vector.
Yes, because two nonzero vectors always span $\mathbb R^3$.

questions.question: Does $((1,0),(0,1),(2,3))$ span $\mathbb R^2$?
options: Yes, but only if $(2,3)$ is removed.
No, because three vectors cannot span $\mathbb R^2$.
No, because $(2,3)$ is not a standard vector.
Yes, because $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ already span $\mathbb R^2$.
